title: AP World History: Key Terms
description: For AP World History learners: key states, people, beliefs, exchanges and transformations from c. 1200 to the present, with selected earlier foundations for context. Original concise explanations for independent review.

sources.name: Original synthesis of established historical knowledge

cards.back: Chinese dynasty ruling 960-1279, associated with commercial expansion, urban growth, civil-service examinations and major technological developments.
Revival and reinterpretation of Confucian thought incorporating responses to Buddhist and Daoist ideas, influential in Song and later East Asia.
Imperial Chinese system selecting many officials through examinations centered on classical learning, reinforcing a scholar-bureaucratic elite.
Educated Chinese elite whose status came from learning, officeholding and often landownership.
Confucian ideal of respect and obligations toward parents and ancestors, extending to wider social hierarchy.
Early-ripening rice introduced into China from Southeast Asia, supporting intensified cultivation and population growth.
Chinese waterway system linking major river basins and facilitating movement of grain, goods and officials.
Practice of tightly binding girls' feet in China, associated with elite femininity and later spreading more broadly; it restricted mobility.
Diplomatic framework in which surrounding rulers offered tribute to an imperial center, often receiving trade access and recognition in return.
Tradition originating in South Asia focused on overcoming suffering and the cycle of rebirth through ethical conduct, insight and spiritual practice.
Broad Buddhist tradition emphasizing the bodhisattva ideal and paths to liberation available to many beings; influential in East Asia.
Buddhist tradition emphasizing monastic discipline and teachings preserved in the Pali canon; influential in Sri Lanka and mainland Southeast Asia.
East Asian Buddhist tradition emphasizing meditation and direct insight; developed from Chinese Chan Buddhism.
Diverse South Asian religious traditions involving concepts such as dharma, karma, rebirth and liberation, with varied devotional and philosophical practices.
South Asian devotional traditions emphasizing personal devotion to a deity, sometimes challenging rigid social or ritual barriers.
Islamic mystical traditions emphasizing spiritual discipline and closeness to God, often organized around teachers and brotherhoods.
A term for lands under Muslim rule or broadly within the Islamic world.
Largest branch of Islam, recognizing the early caliphal succession and emphasizing the community's traditions and scholarly interpretation.
Branch of Islam emphasizing leadership through Ali and his descendants, with diverse traditions concerning legitimate imams.
Islamic normative framework derived from the Quran, prophetic practice and juristic interpretation, applied differently across societies.
Muslim religious scholars who interpret law and religious teachings and often serve educational or judicial roles.
An institution of Islamic learning, often teaching law and religious subjects alongside other fields.
Abbasid-era scholarly institution associated with Baghdad's translation and intellectual culture, especially under al-Mamun.
Islamic dynasty beginning in 750 whose Baghdad-based rule fostered scholarship and commerce; its political authority fragmented over time.
Turkic Muslim dynasty that gained power in Southwest Asia and supported Sunni institutions while reducing Abbasid political authority.
State based in Egypt and Syria, ruled by a military elite of slave origin from 1250 until Ottoman conquest in 1517.
Series of Muslim-ruled states in northern India, 1206-1526, linking South Asia to wider Islamic political and commercial networks.
Hindu-ruled South Indian state founded in the fourteenth century, known for urban wealth, temple patronage and regional warfare.
Southeast Asian empire centered at Angkor, noted for monumental temples and extensive water-management systems.
Major Khmer temple complex in present-day Cambodia, originally dedicated to Vishnu and later used for Buddhist worship.
Maritime Southeast Asian state centered on Sumatra, influential in regional trade and Buddhist networks before its decline.
Java-based state, c. 1293-early sixteenth century, with influence over maritime trade and neighboring islands.
Southern African stone-built urban center, flourishing roughly in the thirteenth-fifteenth centuries, linked to cattle, gold and Indian Ocean trade.
East African coastal trading communities combining African foundations with Islamic and Indian Ocean influences.
Prosperous Swahili port that connected East African gold and other goods to Indian Ocean commerce.
West African empire enriched by gold production and trans-Saharan commerce, especially powerful in the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries.
Fourteenth-century ruler of Mali whose pilgrimage to Mecca displayed imperial wealth and strengthened Islamic connections.
West African commercial and scholarly center associated with Islamic learning and trans-Saharan trade.
West African oral historians and performers who preserve genealogies, political memory and cultural traditions.
Commercial states in West Africa whose cities linked regional production to trans-Saharan exchange.
Long-standing Christian tradition in the Ethiopian highlands, maintained through distinctive institutions and regional political power.
Ethiopian site famous for rock-hewn churches associated with medieval Christian kingship.
A debated term for medieval relationships involving landholding, lordship and service; it describes varied arrangements rather than one uniform system.
Rural economic organization centered on estates where peasants supplied labor or dues to landlords.
Condition in which peasants were legally tied to land or a lord and owed labor or dues, while retaining more rights than enslaved people.
Western Christian institution led by the pope, with major religious, political and cultural influence in medieval Europe.
Christian traditions centered historically on eastern patriarchates and the Byzantine world, distinct from Roman Catholic authority.
Conventional date for the rupture between Roman Catholic and Eastern Orthodox churches, following long-standing theological and political tensions.
Eastern Roman state centered on Constantinople, preserving Roman institutions and Orthodox Christianity until Ottoman conquest in 1453.
Religiously sanctioned military campaigns, especially western European expeditions to the eastern Mediterranean beginning in 1096.
English charter of 1215 limiting some royal actions and affirming certain elite rights; later interpreted as a foundation of constitutional restraint.
English representative institution that developed from royal councils and assemblies, eventually sharing legislative and fiscal authority with the monarchy.
Intermittent conflict between English and French rulers, 1337-1453, contributing to political centralization and military change.
Long series of Christian conquests of Muslim-ruled Iberian territories, conventionally ending with Granada's fall in 1492.
People who built the dominant state in the Aztec Triple Alliance, centered on Tenochtitlan.
Mexica capital on an island in Lake Texcoco, a major urban and ceremonial center conquered by Spanish-led forces in 1521.
Intensive agricultural plots built in shallow lake environments in central Mexico, supporting dense populations.
System requiring subject communities to deliver goods and labor to imperial rulers, supporting the capital and military elite.
Andean empire known as Tawantinsuyu, governed through roads, officials, labor obligations and storage systems before Spanish conquest.
Andean rotational labor obligation used by the Inca state and later adapted coercively by Spanish colonial authorities.
Knotted-cord recording devices used in the Andes, especially for administrative and numerical information.
Inca site in the Andes, generally understood as a royal estate and ceremonial complex.
Large Indigenous urban and ceremonial center near present-day St. Louis, flourishing before and around 1200 within Mississippian culture.
Overland Eurasian trade networks that moved luxury goods, technologies, ideas and pathogens through many intermediaries.
Roadside inn or enclosure sheltering merchants and caravans along major trade routes.
Financial instruments allowing payment across distances, reducing the need to transport large amounts of coin.
Currency issued in paper form, used extensively in medieval China to facilitate exchange and state finance.
Maritime network linking East Africa, the Middle East, South Asia, Southeast Asia and East Asia through seasonal navigation and port commerce.
Seasonally reversing wind patterns that helped sailors plan voyages across the Indian Ocean.
Broad term for traditional sailing vessels used around the Indian Ocean, often associated with lateen sails.
Triangular sail mounted at an angle, improving maneuverability and the ability to sail across the wind.
Navigation instrument indicating magnetic direction, developed in China and spread across Eurasian maritime networks.
Instrument used to determine celestial positions, supporting astronomy, timekeeping and some forms of navigation.
Exchange across the Sahara connecting North Africa and sub-Saharan regions, notably in gold, salt and enslaved people.
Equipment improving camel riding and cargo transport, helping make large-scale desert trade more practical.
Groups of merchants living outside their homeland who maintain commercial and cultural ties across regions.
Fourteenth-century Moroccan traveler whose accounts describe societies across Africa and Eurasia.
Venetian traveler whose account of Asian journeys influenced European knowledge and imagination about the East.
English pilgrim and religious writer whose fifteenth-century account illuminates devotion, travel and women's experiences.
Vast thirteenth-century empire created through Mongol conquest, connecting much of Eurasia under related ruling houses.
Mongol leader who united steppe groups and launched major conquests beginning in the early thirteenth century.
Mongol ruler who founded China's Yuan dynasty and completed the conquest of the Southern Song.
Mongol-ruled Chinese dynasty, 1271-1368, associated with Eurasian connections and a differentiated social hierarchy.
Mongol successor state that dominated much of the western Eurasian steppe and collected tribute from Rus' principalities.
Mongol successor state in Persia and surrounding regions whose rulers later adopted Islam.
Mongol successor state in Central Asia, important in the region's political and cultural transformations.
Term for periods of relative security and commercial integration across Mongol-ruled Eurasia, despite the violence of conquest.
Network of stations providing horses and supplies for official messengers, supporting imperial communication.
Fourteenth-century plague pandemic that killed large portions of populations across parts of Eurasia and North Africa.
A severe population decline caused by factors such as epidemic disease, warfare, famine or forced labor.
Form of plague caused by Yersinia pestis, commonly transmitted through infected fleas and associated with swollen lymph nodes.
Movement of beliefs, practices, technologies and artistic forms between societies.
Blending of elements from different religious or cultural traditions into new forms.
Ming admiral who led large state-sponsored voyages across the Indian Ocean in the early fifteenth century.
Chinese dynasty, 1368-1644, that restored Han Chinese rule after the Yuan and expanded state institutions and commercial activity.
Imperial palace complex in Beijing, central to Ming and Qing political and ceremonial life.
European cultural movement drawing on classical learning and new artistic approaches, first prominent in Italian cities.
Renaissance intellectual emphasis on classical texts, rhetoric, history and human capacities, often compatible with religious belief.
Movable-type printing technology, especially Gutenberg's mid-fifteenth-century European system, which expanded text production and circulation.
Empire built mainly through control of sea routes, ports, islands and overseas colonies.
Network of fortified ports and maritime positions used to influence Indian Ocean commerce rather than govern all surrounding inland territories.
Maneuverable Iberian sailing vessel used in Atlantic exploration, commonly combining features suited to coastal and ocean travel.
Large ocean-going sailing vessel used by Europeans for long-distance trade and exploration.
Portuguese navigator who reached India by sailing around Africa in 1498.
Navigator whose 1492 Atlantic voyage under Spanish sponsorship began sustained European contact with the Americas.
1494 agreement dividing claimed overseas spheres between Spain and Portugal along an Atlantic meridian.
Leader of the expedition begun in 1519 that achieved the first circumnavigation, completed after his death by Juan Sebastian Elcano and survivors.
Transfer of plants, animals, people, pathogens and cultural practices between the Americas and Afro-Eurasia after 1492.
Introduced epidemic disease that caused enormous Indigenous mortality and weakened communities facing European conquest.
Spread of an American staple crop to Africa, Eurasia and other regions, changing diets and agricultural systems.
Spread of an Andean crop that became important for food supplies and population growth in parts of Europe and Asia.
Spanish military adventurers who led expeditions of conquest in the Americas, relying heavily on Indigenous allies and local conflicts.
Spanish leader whose coalition with Indigenous allies defeated the Mexica state in 1521.
Spanish conquistador who led the overthrow of the Inca ruling order amid civil conflict and epidemic disruption.
Spanish colonial grant allowing recipients to demand Indigenous tribute or labor in return for supposed protection and Christian instruction.
Spanish colonial system requiring communities to supply rotating labor quotas, replacing or supplementing earlier labor arrangements.
Large landed estate in Spanish America, often producing crops or livestock through dependent labor relationships.
Large-scale export agriculture organized around coercive labor, especially slavery, and integrated with overseas markets.
Forced transport of millions of Africans across the Atlantic, primarily to labor in American plantation and colonial economies.
Atlantic voyage during which enslaved Africans endured confinement, violence, disease and high mortality.
Simplified model of Atlantic exchange linking Europe, Africa and the Americas; actual routes were more varied.
System treating enslaved people as legally owned property, often making enslaved status hereditary.
Settlements formed by people who escaped slavery, often resisting colonial authorities and preserving distinctive cultures.
Dispersal of African peoples and cultures beyond Africa, profoundly shaped by forced Atlantic migration.
Colonial Spanish American practices of classifying people by ancestry and status, with categories that were influential but not wholly fixed.
People born in Iberia who lived in Spanish or Portuguese American colonies, often holding privileged positions.
People of European descent born in the Americas, many of whom became leaders of independence movements.
Colonial category commonly referring to mixed Indigenous American and European ancestry, with meanings varying by place and time.
Policies seeking state power through favorable trade, regulated commerce, colonial production and accumulation of wealth.
Business organization in which investors pool capital and share risks and profits through ownership shares.
Chartered Dutch company founded in 1602 with extensive commercial and political powers in Asian trade.
English company founded in 1600 that expanded from Asian commerce into territorial rule in South Asia.
Major silver-mining center in present-day Bolivia whose output supplied Spanish imperial and global trade networks.
Ships linking Spanish America and the Philippines, carrying American silver westward and Asian goods eastward.
Early modern movement of American and Japanese silver through world markets, with strong demand in China.
Sustained inflation in sixteenth-century Europe associated with population growth, monetary changes and precious-metal inflows.
Empire centered on Anatolia and later Istanbul, governing much of Southeast Europe, Southwest Asia and North Africa.
Ottoman sultan who conquered Constantinople in 1453 and strengthened imperial centralization.
Sixteenth-century Ottoman sultan associated with territorial expansion, legal organization and cultural patronage.
Ottoman levy that recruited Christian boys from some imperial territories for conversion, training and service in military or administrative roles.
Elite Ottoman infantry corps historically linked to the devshirme system and direct service to the sultan.
Term for Ottoman arrangements granting religious communities certain administrative and legal roles; its structure changed over time.
Persian empire founded in 1501 that established Twelver Shiism as a major state identity.
Founder of the Safavid dynasty who promoted Twelver Shia Islam in Persia.
1514 Ottoman victory over the Safavids, demonstrating the importance of Ottoman firearms and shaping regional rivalry.
Dynasty founded in South Asia in 1526 that combined military expansion, Persianate court culture and varied policies toward religious diversity.
Mughal emperor known for expansion, administrative reforms and efforts to incorporate religiously diverse elites.
Mughal emperor whose long reign expanded the empire while intensifying military pressures and some religious restrictions.
South Asian local landholding or revenue-collecting elites whose roles varied under Mughal and later British systems.
Comparative label often applied to the Ottoman, Safavid and Mughal empires because firearms supported expansion and central rule, alongside many other factors.
Manchu-ruled Chinese dynasty, 1644-1912, that expanded imperial territory and combined Manchu institutions with Chinese administrative traditions.
Long-reigning Qing ruler who consolidated power and supported territorial expansion and scholarly projects.
Eighteenth-century Qing ruler associated with territorial expansion, cultural patronage and late-reign strains on government.
Japanese military government, 1603-1868, that stabilized daimyo relations, regulated foreign contact and presided over commercial growth.
Regional Japanese lords who controlled domains and maintained warrior retainers.
Japanese warrior status group that increasingly served administrative roles during the Tokugawa peace.
Tokugawa alternate-attendance system requiring daimyo to spend regular periods in Edo, helping the shogunate control them.
Label for Tokugawa restrictions on foreign contact; Japan maintained limited, regulated connections rather than complete isolation.
Growth of Russian rule across Siberia and other regions, driven by security, settlement, tribute and resources such as fur.
Russian ruler who promoted military and administrative reforms, European contacts and a new capital at St. Petersburg.
Russian empress who expanded territory and patronized Enlightenment ideas while preserving autocracy and noble privilege.
Model of monarchy claiming concentrated sovereign authority, although rulers still faced practical institutional and social limits.
Belief that a monarch's authority comes from God and should not be challenged by subjects.
French king whose long reign symbolized royal centralization, court culture and ambitious warfare.
French royal palace and court complex used by Louis XIV to display power and organize elite life around the monarchy.
Sixteenth-century movements challenging Roman Catholic doctrine and authority, producing several Protestant traditions.
German reformer whose criticisms of indulgences and teachings on faith and scripture helped launch the Protestant Reformation.
Remissions of temporal punishment for sin in Catholic teaching; abuses in their promotion helped spark Reformation controversy.
Protestant reformer associated with Geneva and teachings emphasizing divine sovereignty and predestination.
Separation of the English church from papal authority under Henry VIII, followed by further religious changes under later rulers.
Catholic renewal and response to Protestantism through doctrinal clarification, institutional reform and new religious orders.
Catholic council, 1545-1563, that reaffirmed doctrines and enacted reforms in response to Protestant challenges.
Catholic religious order founded in the sixteenth century, influential in education, missions and the Catholic Reformation.
European conflict, 1618-1648, involving religious and dynastic rivalries and devastating much of Central Europe.
1648 settlements ending major European wars, adjusting political and confessional arrangements within the Holy Roman Empire and beyond.
Early modern transformation in European natural inquiry involving new mathematical models, instruments and methods of observation.
Model placing the sun near the center of planetary motions rather than Earth, advanced in early modern Europe by Copernicus and others.
Scientist whose telescopic observations and work on motion challenged inherited views and brought conflict with Catholic authorities.
Scientist who formulated laws of motion and universal gravitation, unifying major features of terrestrial and celestial mechanics.
Eighteenth-century intellectual movement emphasizing reason, critical inquiry and debate about authority, rights and social improvement.
Thinker associated with natural rights, government by consent and the possibility of resisting governments that violate their purposes.
Idea that political authority rests on an agreement, actual or hypothetical, among people establishing rules and government.
Enlightenment writer associated with separating governmental powers to limit arbitrary rule.
Enlightenment writer who criticized intolerance and defended religious toleration and freedom of thought.
Political thinker associated with popular sovereignty and the general will, influential in later revolutionary thought.
Writer who argued for women's education and rational equality in A Vindication of the Rights of Woman.
Colonial struggle that produced independence from Britain and a republic in the United States, 1775-1783.
1776 statement announcing American independence and invoking equality, natural rights and consent of the governed.
Political and social upheaval beginning in 1789 that challenged monarchy and privilege and produced successive revolutionary governments.
French representative assembly of clergy, nobility and commoners whose 1789 meeting helped trigger revolutionary change.

cards.front: Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen
cards.back: 1789 French statement asserting liberty, legal equality and national sovereignty, while not granting equal political rights to all residents.
Period of revolutionary emergency rule and extensive political executions in France, principally 1793-1794.
French military ruler who consolidated some revolutionary reforms while establishing an empire and waging extensive European wars.
French civil code that standardized law and protected property and male civil equality while reinforcing patriarchal family authority.
Revolution beginning in 1791 that overthrew slavery and French colonial rule, producing independent Haiti in 1804.
Major leader of the Haitian Revolution who built military and political power before being captured by the French.
Haitian revolutionary leader who declared independence in 1804 after the defeat of French forces.
Leader of independence struggles in northern South America who sought broad regional political unity.
Leader of independence campaigns in southern South America, especially Argentina, Chile and Peru.
Priest whose 1810 uprising helped initiate Mexico's independence struggle.
Belief that a people sharing a national identity should possess political unity or self-government.
Political tradition emphasizing individual rights, constitutional government and legal equality, with changing views on suffrage and economic policy.
Political outlook favoring established institutions and gradual change, especially influential in reaction to revolution.
1814-1815 settlement seeking European stability and a balance of power after Napoleon's defeat.
Wave of European uprisings pursuing varied liberal, nationalist and social demands, many initially suppressed.
Nineteenth-century process creating a unified Italian kingdom through diplomacy, war and popular movements.
Process culminating in the German Empire in 1871 under Prussian leadership following diplomacy and wars.
Prussian statesman who used diplomacy and limited wars to advance German unification and preserve conservative authority.
Transition toward mechanized production and new energy systems that began in Britain and spread unevenly worldwide.
Consolidation and privatization of common or open-field land in Britain, changing agriculture and rural livelihoods.
Machine converting steam's energy into mechanical work, central to industrial production, mining and transport.
Production organized around concentrated machinery and wage labor under centralized management.
Mechanization of spinning and weaving that helped lead early industrial growth and increased demand for cotton.
Coal, oil and natural gas, whose large-scale use transformed industrial energy supplies and environmental impacts.
Transport networks that lowered land-shipping costs, integrated markets and supported state and imperial expansion.
Late nineteenth- and early twentieth-century expansion in steel, chemicals, electricity and other new industries.
Growth in the proportion of people living in towns and cities, accelerated by industrial employment and migration.
People who primarily earn livelihoods through wage labor, especially industrial workers in nineteenth-century contexts.
Term for middle or capitalist classes, especially owners of productive property in Marxist analysis.
Economic system centered on private ownership, markets and investment for profit, operating in varied political settings.
Scottish thinker whose work analyzed markets, specialization and political economy, including criticisms of mercantilist restrictions.
Principle favoring limited governmental interference in economic activity.
Family of ideas favoring social or collective control of major productive resources and greater economic equality.
Thinker who analyzed capitalism through class conflict and envisioned its replacement by a classless communist society.
1848 work by Marx and Engels presenting class struggle and calling for workers' revolutionary organization.
Organizations of workers seeking improved wages, conditions and bargaining power.
Nineteenth-century British working-class movement demanding parliamentary and voting reforms through the People's Charter.
Movements seeking to end slavery and, in some contexts, the slave trade.
Movement and principle supporting women's right to vote.
1848 gathering in New York that called for women's rights, including suffrage.
1868 political transformation restoring formal imperial authority in Japan and enabling extensive state-led modernization.
Japanese state-supported development of industry, infrastructure, education and military capacity in the late nineteenth century.
Large Japanese family-controlled business conglomerates that grew prominent during industrialization.
Ottoman reform era, 1839-1876, seeking administrative, legal and military modernization and a stronger imperial state.
Nineteenth-century Qing effort to adopt selected foreign military and industrial techniques while preserving much of the existing order.
Nineteenth-century wars involving Britain and later France against Qing China, resulting in expanded foreign commercial privileges.
1842 agreement ending the First Opium War, opening treaty ports and ceding Hong Kong Island to Britain.
Treaties imposed under pressure that granted foreign powers privileges and constrained states such as Qing China.
Massive mid-nineteenth-century uprising against Qing rule led by a movement with a distinctive Christian-influenced ideology.
Anti-foreign and anti-Christian movement in China around 1899-1901, suppressed by an international military coalition.
Late nineteenth-century expansion of European and other powers' control over territories, markets and peoples.
Rapid partition and conquest of much of Africa by European powers in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries.
1884-1885 European-led conference establishing rules concerning African colonization and trade without meaningful African representation.
Application of distorted ideas of biological competition to justify social hierarchy, racism or imperial domination.
Imperial claim that colonial rule would improve colonized peoples, used to legitimize domination and cultural coercion.
Territory personally controlled by Leopold II of Belgium, notorious for violent forced labor and rubber extraction.
Belgian monarch whose personal rule in the Congo generated immense abuses before Belgian state annexation in 1908.
Waterway opened in 1869 connecting the Mediterranean and Red seas, transforming travel and imperial strategy.
Large uprising against East India Company rule that led Britain to impose direct crown rule over India.
Period of direct British crown rule in India, 1858-1947, structured through colonial administration and princely states.
Indian soldiers employed in European colonial armies, especially those of the British East India Company and British India.
Foreign domination through investment, debt, trade or business control without necessarily establishing direct colonial government.
Colonialism involving substantial settlement by outsiders who displace or subordinate Indigenous populations and claim land.
Labor performed under a contract for a fixed term, often with severe coercion or exploitation in colonial migration systems.
Immigration restrictions targeting Chinese migrants, exemplified by the United States' Chinese Exclusion Act of 1882.
Conditions encouraging people to leave, such as poverty, violence, land pressure or persecution.
Conditions attracting migrants, such as employment, land, family networks or perceived safety.
Global conflict of 1914-1918 centered on rival European alliances, fought through industrialized warfare and imperial mobilization.
Interlocking agreements that increased the risk of a regional conflict expanding into a wider war.
Combat organized around fortified positions, especially associated with the stalemated Western Front in World War I.
Warfare mobilizing a society's economic and civilian resources and blurring boundaries between military and civilian targets.
Mass killing and deportation of Armenians by Ottoman authorities during World War I.
Revolutions that overthrew the tsar and later brought the Bolsheviks to power.
Revolutionary socialist faction led by Lenin that seized power in Russia in October 1917 by the Russian calendar then in use.
Bolshevik leader who directed the revolutionary seizure of power and helped establish the Soviet state.
1919 peace treaty with Germany imposing territorial changes, military limits and reparations after World War I.
International organization created after World War I to promote cooperation and collective security, weakened by limited participation and enforcement.
League of Nations framework assigning former German and Ottoman territories to other powers under purported international oversight.
Severe worldwide economic downturn beginning around 1929, marked by unemployment, falling production and disrupted trade.
Approach emphasizing aggregate demand and the role of public policy in stabilizing employment and output.
United States programs under Franklin Roosevelt responding to the Great Depression through relief, recovery and reform.
Authoritarian ultranationalist politics rejecting liberal democracy and emphasizing hierarchy, militarism and a mobilized national community.
Leader of Italian Fascism who established a dictatorship and pursued imperial expansion.
German fascist ideology centered on dictatorship, racial hierarchy, antisemitism and territorial expansion.
Nazi leader whose dictatorship initiated aggressive war in Europe and organized genocidal policies including the Holocaust.
Policy of making concessions to avoid conflict, associated with British and French responses to Nazi expansion before World War II.
Global war, 1939-1945 in Europe and with earlier roots in Asia, ending in Axis defeat and major shifts in world power.
Nazi Germany's systematic genocide of approximately six million Jews; the regime also persecuted and murdered other groups.
Mass killing, sexual violence and other atrocities committed by Japanese forces after capturing Nanjing in 1937.
United States attacks on Hiroshima and Nagasaki in August 1945, causing mass destruction and helping shape the war's end and nuclear age.
International organization founded in 1945 to promote peace, security, cooperation and human rights.
1948 UN declaration articulating a broad set of rights and freedoms for all people.
Global rivalry between the United States and Soviet Union and their allies, involving ideological competition, arms races and proxy conflicts.
United States strategy seeking to limit the expansion of Soviet influence and communism.
United States aid program supporting European economic recovery after World War II.
Military alliance founded in 1949 around collective defense, initially linking North America and Western Europe.
Soviet-led military alliance formed in 1955 among Eastern European communist states.
Process through which colonies gained independence, often through negotiation, mass mobilization or armed struggle.
End of British rule in 1947 and division into India and Pakistan, accompanied by large-scale migration and communal violence.
Indian nationalist leader associated with nonviolent resistance and campaigns against British colonial rule.
Association of states seeking independence from formal alignment with either Cold War bloc.
Victory of Mao Zedong's communist forces in 1949 and establishment of the People's Republic of China.
Chinese campaign beginning in 1958 for rapid collectivization and industrialization that contributed to catastrophic famine.
Mao-led upheaval, 1966-1976, attacking perceived ideological enemies and causing persecution and severe institutional disruption.
South African system of legally enforced racial segregation and white-minority domination, formally dismantled in the early 1990s.
Anti-apartheid leader and South Africa's first president elected in a fully multiracial national election in 1994.
Spread of high-yield crop varieties, fertilizers, irrigation and related techniques, increasing harvests while creating social and environmental tradeoffs.
Intensification of cross-border connections in trade, finance, migration, communication and culture.
Policy orientation emphasizing market competition, privatization, deregulation and reduced state roles in some economic activities.
Breakup of the Soviet Union in 1991 into independent states, marking the end of its Cold War superpower role.
Long-term shifts in climate; recent global warming is driven mainly by human greenhouse-gas emissions and has worldwide political and environmental consequences.
